sweep_summary: Only one works with stress in the title for halh1238: Hagberg 2006 (SIL e-Books 3) = Hagberg 1993 University of Arizona dissertation 'An autosegmental theory of stress'. The Glottolog handle (MPG pure) and sil.org were bot-blocked (not reachable by automated download), but an open scan of the 1993 dissertation is on archive.org (item an-autosegmental-theory-of-stress, third-party upload 2025); PDF (365 pp., text layer) and scanned text with and updated. Khalkha occupies pp. 192-195: rule 'first long vowel stressed, else first vowel', data from Street 1963, analysed as Weight-to-Stress (left-to-right, non-iterative) + End Rule Left. This is secondary (Street's data) and confirms the catalog's 'weight' coding; it refines the deciding Poppe 1970 quote only for words with 3+ long vowels (leftmost vs. penultimate long vowel), where Walker 1997's 'rightmost nonfinal heavy' also differs. It does not supersede Poppe/Walker. Also re-read the first-hand acoustic papers already held by the project from the 9/16 check: Svantesson 1990 (intensity: first long vowel else initial; concludes no unified word stress), Sang & Martin 2012 (F0 highest on the long vowel, else initial; stress position predictable), Karlsson & Svantesson 2004 (reject lexical stress, prominence phrasal). Nothing left unacquired for this item; priority none.

new_statements.reading: weight-sensitive unbounded system: stress the leftmost long vowel; if the word has no long vowel, stress the initial syllable. Agrees with the catalog's 'weight' kind and with Poppe 1970 for words with zero, one or two long vowels (Poppe's 'penultimate long vowel' and Hagberg/Street's 'first long vowel' coincide for two); they diverge only for three or more long vowels (leftmost vs. penultimate), and Hagberg's data contain no such word. Not first-hand: the six forms are taken from Street 1963. The only first-hand statements read in this search of works with stress in the title are the on-disk instrumental papers: Svantesson 1990 (intensity peaks on the first long vowel else the initial vowel, but 'a unified phenomenon of word stress does not exist'), Sang & Martin 2012 (F0 highest on the long vowel, else initial), and Karlsson & Svantesson 2004 (reject lexical stress; prominence is phrasal).

new_statements.quote: Although STKF do not commit themselves as to where main word stress is ('our conclusion is that word stress is not phonologically relevant in Mongolian' (p. 96)), one might infer that since the long-short vowel contrast is only in the initial syllable, this is where stress is located.3 [fn. 3:] This is indeed 'the opinion of almost all native Mongolian scholars' (p. 96). The stress rule assumed for Halh by Hayes (1980) (based on Street (1963), and most subsequent work in generative phonology, is that stress falls on the first long vowel (e.g. long initial vowel or full non-initial vowel), otherwise on the first syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Per the monograph as quoted by its reviewer: word stress is not phonologically relevant in (Halh) Mongolian; the reviewer notes that native Mongolian scholars place stress on the initial syllable and that the Street/Hayes generative rule is first long vowel, else first syllable.

new_statements.identity_note: Nevins/Svantesson et al. describe Halh, the standard dialect of Ulaanbaatar. Hagberg's data are Khalkha (Street 1963). Amraa 1993 teaches the modern standard language, which it says is based on the Halh dialect. Schmidt 1831 describes the written (literary) Mongolian of his day and its pronunciation, not the Halh dialect specifically; its examples are Classical Mongolian forms. Ujiyediin 1998 is based on Inner Mongolian materials and says nothing about stress.

new_statements.quote: §. 26. Bei weitem die meisten zwei- und dreisylbigen Mongolischen Wörter haben den Accent auf der ersten Sylbe, als z. B. ende „hier", Mongghol, üssük „Buchstab, Schreibfeder", nomlacho „lehren", naran „die Sonne", ssara „der Mond". §. 27. Eine Ausnahme machen in der Regel diejenigen Wörter, in welchen die zweite oder dritte Sylbe durch einen weichen Guttural gebildet, oder durch einen Diphthong oder j verlängert wird, als z. B. degö „der jüngere Bruder", dschige „der Schwiegersohn", daghon „die Stimme", naghor „der See, Teich", aghola „der Berg", abchogholcho „nehmen lassen", takja „die Henne", kerje „die Krähe", ukjal „das Bad", ügei „nicht, nein", ugju der Edelstein Ju [...].
new_statements.translation: §26. By far most two- and three-syllable Mongolian words have the accent on the first syllable, e.g. ende 'here', Mongghol, üssük 'letter, pen', nomlacho 'to teach', naran 'the sun', ssara 'the moon'. §27. As a rule, an exception is made by those words in which the second or third syllable is formed with a soft guttural, or is lengthened by a diphthong or j, e.g. degö 'the younger brother', dschige 'the son-in-law', daghon 'the voice', naghor 'the lake, pond', aghola 'the mountain', abchogholcho 'to have (someone) take', takja 'the hen', kerje 'the crow', ukjal 'the bath', ügei 'not, no', ugju the gem Ju [...]. (In the printed examples the accented vowel carries a macron: ēnde, nōmlacho, nāran, ssāra; degō, dschigē, daghōn, naghōr, aghōla, abchoghōlcho, takjā, kerjē, ukjāl, ügēi, ugjū.)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent on the first syllable by default; it moves to a second or third syllable that is long, i.e. one formed with a 'soft guttural' (the VgV/VγV sequences that yield the modern long vowels), a diphthong or a j-glide. In substance this is 'stress the (first) long vowel, else the initial syllable'.
new_statements.exceptions: The 'exception' class in sec. 27 is the rule's weight condition (long non-initial syllable takes the accent); no lexical exceptions listed.

readall_conflicts: The descriptive and generative tradition (Schmidt 1831 secs. 26-27 for the written language; Street 1963 via Hagberg 1993/2006, pp. 192-195) places stress on the first long syllable, else the initial syllable. The one first-hand modern phonology among the listed works, Svantesson, Tsendina, Karlsson & Franzen 2005, could only be reached through Nevins's 2009 review, which quotes the book's p. 96 verbatim: 'our conclusion is that word stress is not phonologically relevant in Mongolian'; the reviewer adds that native Mongolian scholars favour initial stress. So the sources disagree on the type (phonologically relevant weight-sensitive stress vs. no phonologically relevant word stress), not on where prominence is heard: Svantesson's own instrumental work already held by the project (1990) finds intensity peaks on the first long vowel else the initial vowel, which is the same location. Amraa 1993 and Ujiyediin 1998 are silent.

audit.recode_to: Mark as CONTESTED / no-lexical-stress candidate: keep Poppe 1970 + Walker 1997 as the source of the quantity-sensitive 'rightmost nonfinal CVV, else initial' rule but add a caution that the instrumental literature on Halh (Svantesson 1990; Karlsson & Svantesson 2004; Karlsson 2005; Svantesson et al. 2005) finds no unified word stress (phrasal LH accent on the first two morae) and that the one instrumental study that does posit word stress (Sang & Martin 2012, 4 UB speakers) finds leftmost-heavy-else-initial, not rightmost-nonfinal. If the catalog has a 'none/phrasal' or 'contested' kind, move halh1238 there (or set not in the strict set + caution and drop 'edge: unbounded rightmost' to 'edge: disputed L vs R'); final call after reading Svantesson et al. 2005 ch. on word stress (~p.85-97) and Karlsson 2005.

sources.quote: '1. Stress falls on the first syllable for the words with only short vowels. 2. Stress falls on the leftmost syllable containing a long vowel.' In words with several long vowels 'the leftmost long vowel has always the highest Fo value, the longest vowel duration'. Weight-sensitive (CVV) as coded, but leftmost-heavy-else-initial, not Walker's rightmost-nonfinal-heavy.

Supports weight-sensitive placement with initial default.

sources.note: General theory dissertation (Mayo is the main case study); Khalkha is one of six 'unbounded' types, treated on ~3 pages with data credited to Street 1963 (Khalkha Structure), not first-hand. Rule stated: stress the first (leftmost) long vowel; if no long vowel, the first vowel. Analysed as Weight-to-Stress applied non-iteratively left-to-right + End Rule Left, no feet. Weight = long vowel only (no mention of closed syllables or diphthongs).

sources.quote: Although STKF do not commit themselves as to where main word stress is ('our conclusion is that word stress is not phonologically relevant in Mongolian' (p. 96)), one might infer that since the long-short vowel contrast is only in the initial syllable, this is where stress is located.3 [fn. 3:] This is indeed 'the opinion of almost all native Mongolian scholars' (p. 96). The stress rule assumed for Halh by Hayes (1980) (based on Street (1963), and most subsequent work in generative phonology, is that stress falls on the first long vowel (e.g. long initial vowel or full non-initial vowel), otherwise on the first syllable.
sources.locator: Nevins 2009, Phonology 26(3): 526 and fn. 3 (PDF p. 3 of the DASH file); the book itself is cited at its p. 96 and ch. 7
sources.note: The standard phonology of Halh; its word-stress section (around p.96, six competing descriptions tabulated) concludes stress is not phonologically relevant and analyses non-initial long vowels as short, undermining both the placement rule and the CVV-heavy basis our 'weight' coding takes from a 1970 handbook paragraph.

sources.citation: Karlsson, Anastasia Mukhanova & Jan-Olof Svantesson. 2004. Prominence and mora in Mongolian. Speech Prosody 2004 (Nara). doi:10.21437/SpeechProsody.2004-15
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'Basing ourself on this investigation we reject the existence of lexical stress in Mongolian and find prominence as functioning only at the phrasal level'; focal/word accent is a bitonal LH gesture aligned with the first two morae; long vowels analysed as occurring only in initial syllables (non-initial 'long' vowels = phonemic short, short = epenthetic schwa), which removes the CVV weight basis of the Poppe/Walker rule outside syllable 1.
sources.locator: sec. 1 Introduction and sec. 2-3; Halh speakers, read speech
sources.note: Rejects lexical (word) stress for Halh; prominence is phrasal (LH gesture anchored to the second mora of the phrase-initial word). Long vowels count two morae; only initial syllables carry phonemic vowels.

sources.citation: Svantesson, Jan-Olof. 1990. Phonetic correlates of stress in Mongolian. Proceedings of ICSLP 90 (Kobe), vol. 1, 617-620. doi:10.21437/ICSLP.1990-178
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Abstract: 'The conclusion is that a unified phenomenon of word stress does not exist in Mongolian.' Discussion: 'The four parameters considered here do not cooccur to give prominence to any fixed syllable of a Mongolian word'; intensity data 'the first long vowel of the word has highest intensity, and if there are no long vowels, the initial vowel has highest intensity' (= Poppe 1951 rule: first long vowel else initial, not Poppe 1970 penultimate/rightmost); F0 Low-High 'tied to the first two moras' and judged phrasal.
sources.locator: pp.617-619 (abstract, Discussion, Conclusion); 3 Ulaanbaatar Khalkha speakers, duration/F1-F2/intensity/F0
sources.note: First-hand instrumental study (3 speakers, standard Khalkha). Intensity peaks on the first long vowel, else the initial vowel (matches Street/Hagberg, and Poppe for words with <=2 long vowels); duration and vowel quality favour the initial syllable; F0 patterns differ by speaker. Concludes no unified word stress exists.

sources.quote: Adopts Walker 1997 (rightmost non-final heavy, else initial) as the working description but reports: Svantesson et al. 2005 'point this out, stating "there are widely differing opinions on the place and nature of word stress in Mongolian" (p. 96), exemplifying at least six different opinions'; argues initial default prominence is intonational, not foot-based (after Gordon 2000; Svantesson et al. 2005). Secondary; no new native-speaker production data on placement.
